EDCS-33800001.text_edition: \n Smertulitano deo Lucius Victorius Censorinus sacerdos eiusdem numinis dedit dedicavit et fibulas duas inauravit\n
EDCS-33800001.translation: To the god Smertulitanus, Lucius Victorius Censorinus, priest of the same divinity, gave and dedicated it, and gilded two fibulae.
EDCS-33800001.summary: This is a dedication by a priest to the god Smertulitanus, mentioning the dedication of the monument and two gilded fibulae.

EDCS-33800004.text_edition: \n Imperatori Caesari Lucio Septimio Severo Pio Pertinaci Augusto Arabico Adiab<e=I>(nico) Parthico maximo patri patriae consuli III et Imperatori Caesari Marco Aurelio Anto<n=A>ino Pio Felici consuli et Publio Septimio Getae nobilissimo Caesari a Tarvenna leugas XIV \n
EDCS-33800004.translation: To Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Pius Pertinax Augustus, Arabicus, Adiabenicus, Parthicus Maximus, father of the fatherland, consul for the third time, and to Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Pius Felix, consul, and to Publius Septimius Geta, most noble Caesar, from Tarenna, 14 leagues.
EDCS-33800004.summary: This inscription records distances, likely milestones, related to the reigns of Emperors Septimius Severus, Caracalla, and Geta.

EDCS-33800010.summary: This inscription records a sale or price of asparagus by Ianuarius Ciutus for one denarius.

EDCS-33800011.summary: This inscription likely records the sale of a sparrow, possibly as food or a pet, with its weight and price.

EDCS-33800012.summary: This inscription records the sale of cooked sparrow, specifying its weight.

EDCS-33800013.translation: Quadratus: coracinus fish, 7 pounds, 3 and a half denarii.
EDCS-33800013.summary: This inscription records the sale of a coracinus fish by Quadratus, specifying its weight and price.

EDCS-33800014.translation: To the spirits of the underworld, for Marcellinus the slave dealer.
EDCS-33800014.summary: This is a funerary inscription dedicated to Marcellinus, a slave dealer, likely dating to the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-33800015.summary: This inscription is fragmented and appears to be a funerary dedication, possibly for an individual named Vitalis, with missing text indicating his status or relation.

EDCS-33800018.translation: Ori[---] Nicamede stole it from the pine tree [---]. And he will have a remedy if he made it himself [---] he will return it if he sends it himself. [---] and Pinnire edio and in veneri
EDCS-33800018.summary: This inscription appears to be a curse or a warning related to the theft of an object, possibly found in Nicamede's possession, with conditions for its return.

EDCS-36300084.translation: Galba dedicated this to the god Mercury in fulfillment of a vow.
EDCS-36300084.summary: This is a votive inscription recording that Galba dedicated a monument to the god Mercury.

EDCS-37700220.summary: This is a personal inscription, likely a name or a fragment of a longer dedication, identifying Quintus Valerius Sabe().

EDCS-46600048.translation: To the Great Mother of the Gods, Arcadius, a haruspex, son of Patricius, consumed by [his vow], having made his vows.
EDCS-46600048.summary: A dedication to Magna Mater by Arcadius, a haruspex, likely from the Roman Imperial period.

EDCS-46600049.translation: She who lies under this stone, with motherly morals, fair to all, and sharing in everyone's grief, the chaste Boethiola, nobly born, a most illustrious woman, wife of Amandus, who erected this inscription. Oh, how savage the day that inflicted sixteen years upon her, during which she lived chastely with her own husband. Boethiola, most illustrious woman, lived 25 years, 9 months, and 3 days; she was the wife of Amandus, a most distinguished man, for 12 years and 19 days.
EDCS-46600049.summary: A funerary epitaph for Boethiola, wife of Amandus, detailing her age, marital status, and character, likely from the later Roman Empire.

EDCS-46600050.text_edition: \n Exsuperantius sic Pissitus vixit annos XXXV Sanct<i=E> martyres et beata spirita suscipite spiritum Exsuperanti sic cum pace locus ex voto \n
EDCS-46600050.translation: Exsuperantius thus lived 35 years. Holy martyrs and blessed spirits, receive the spirit of Exsuperantius. May there be a place with peace, according to the vow.
EDCS-46600050.summary: A Christian funerary inscription for Exsuperantius, requesting reception by holy martyrs and spirits, likely from the 4th or 5th century CE.

EDCS-46600054.translation: For Sucaria, of chaste character, who lived 43 years. Deposited in peace on the 15th day before the Kalends of September.
EDCS-46600054.summary: A Christian funerary epitaph for Sucaria, noting her age and date of burial, likely from the late Roman Empire or early Byzantine period.

EDCS-46600055.translation: Severus and Kalendia placed [this] for their most sweet daughter Paula, against [their] vow. She lived in Christ 8 months and 3 days.
EDCS-46600055.summary: A Christian funerary epitaph for Paula, erected by her parents Severus and Kalendia, detailing her short life, likely from the 4th or 5th century CE.

EDCS-46600056.translation: For Aurelia, a most sweet infant, who lived two years, four months, and eight days. She rests in peace. Amandus and Servanda, her parents, placed this inscription for their dearest [daughter].
EDCS-46600056.summary: A Christian funerary epitaph for Aurelia, a young child, erected by her parents Amandus and Servanda, likely from the late Roman Empire or early Byzantine period.

EDCS-46600057.text_edition: \n Urbiciae infanti dulc<i=E>ssimae quae recessit X Kalendas Novembres nnorum II mensium IIII dierum V \n
EDCS-46600057.translation: For Urbicia, a most sweet infant, who departed on the 10th day before the Kalends of November, aged 2 years, 4 months, and 5 days.
EDCS-46600057.summary: A Christian funerary epitaph for the infant Urbicia, noting her age and date of death, likely from the late Roman Empire or early Byzantine period.

EDCS-46600058.translation: Florus rests in peace, faithful, who lived 10 years, 2 months, and 27 days, buried on the 12th day before the Kalends of February.
